references.text: Elijah was taken up to heaven, and the expectation that he would return lies behind the popular speculation that Elijah had appeared.
Malachi prophesies that Elijah will be sent before the Lord's great and dreadful day, which formed the basis for the people's speculation that Elijah had appeared.
When Jesus asks his disciples who people say he is, the same speculations are repeated: John the Baptist, Elijah, or one of the old prophets raised up again.
Mark's parallel where the people say that Jesus is Elijah, or a prophet like one of the old prophets.
Matthew's parallel where the disciples report that some say Jesus is Elijah or one of the prophets.
Moses' promise that the Lord will raise up a prophet like him from among the people, which lies behind the expectation that one of the old prophets would rise again.
The people reacted to Jesus' miracles by saying that a great prophet has risen among them—the same kind of reaction mentioned in 9:8.
The questions asked of John the Baptist about whether he was Elijah or the Prophet show the same messianic expectations that lay behind the popular talk about Jesus.
